\begin{frame}{Why tests are important}
\protect\phantomsection\label{why-tests-are-important}
\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Risk Mitigation

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Testing helps identify defects and failures early in the development
    process when they are less expensive to fix. This reduces project
    risks related to quality, security, performance, etc.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Confidence

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Executing a well--planned software test strategy provides confidence
    that the software works as intended before its release.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Compliance

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Testing can ensure that software adheres to standards, regulations,
    and compliance requirements. This is especially critical for
    safety--critical systems.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  User Satisfaction

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Rigorous testing from a user perspective can verify usability,
    functionality, and compatibility. This increases customer/user
    satisfaction and reduces negative impacts to an organization's
    reputation or finances from poor quality products.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Why tests are important}
\protect\phantomsection\label{why-tests-are-important-1}
\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Optimization

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Testing provides vital feedback that can be used to continuously
    improve software quality, user experience, security, performance and
    other product attributes.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Cost Savings

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Investing in testing activities reduces downstream costs related to
    defects found post--release. It is much cheaper to find and fix bugs
    earlier in the development cycle.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\ldots{} and many more reasons
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Why tests are important (SW developer perspective)}
\protect\phantomsection\label{why-tests-are-important-sw-developer-perspective}
\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Enable us testing corner case scenarios

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Testing enables us to validate that our code behaves correctly under
    various conditions, including edge cases.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Ensure code stability

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Testing helps maintain code stability by catching regressions and
    unintended side effects early in the development process.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Facilitate refactoring and code maintenance

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Testing allows developers to confidently refactor and maintain code,
    knowing that existing functionality is protected by a suite of
    automated tests.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Why tests are important (SW developer perspective)}
\protect\phantomsection\label{why-tests-are-important-sw-developer-perspective-1}
\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  They are instant!

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Unit tests can be executed quickly (often in seconds or minutes),
    providing immediate feedback to developers about the correctness of
    their code.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Disclaimer}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    They took time to write and maintain. Often it is 2x time of
    development. But AI can help significantly!
  \item
    Unit tests are not a silver bullet; they complement other testing
    types and practices to ensure overall software quality.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Different types of (automated) testing}
\protect\phantomsection\label{different-types-of-automated-testing}
\begin{block}{Unit tests}
\protect\phantomsection\label{unit-tests}
Unit tests are very low level and close to the source of an application.
They consist in testing individual methods and functions of the classes,
components, or modules used by your software. Unit tests are generally
quite cheap to automate and can run very quickly by a continuous
integration server.
\end{block}

\begin{block}{Integration tests}
\protect\phantomsection\label{integration-tests}
Integration tests verify that different modules or services used by your
application work well together. For example, it can be testing the
interaction with the database or making sure that microservices work
together as expected. These types of tests are more expensive to run as
they require multiple parts of the application to be up and running.
\end{block}

\begin{block}{Functional tests}
\protect\phantomsection\label{functional-tests}
Functional tests focus on the business requirements of an application.
They only verify the output of an action and do not check the
intermediate states of the system when performing that action. There is
sometimes a confusion between integration tests and functional tests as
they both require multiple components to interact with each other. The
difference is that an integration test may simply verify that you can
query the database while a functional test would expect to get a
specific value from the database as defined by the product requirements.
\end{block}

\begin{block}{End-to-end tests}
\protect\phantomsection\label{end-to-end-tests}
End-to-end testing replicates a user behavior with the software in a
complete application environment. It verifies that various user flows
work as expected and can be as simple as loading a web page or logging
in or much more complex scenarios verifying email notifications, online
payments, etc\ldots{} End-to-end tests are very useful, but they're
expensive to perform and can be hard to maintain when they're automated.
It is recommended to have a few key end-to-end tests and rely more on
lower level types of testing (unit and integration tests) to be able to
quickly identify breaking changes.
\end{block}

\begin{block}{Acceptance testing}
\protect\phantomsection\label{acceptance-testing}
Acceptance tests are formal tests that verify if a system satisfies
business requirements. They require the entire application to be running
while testing and focus on replicating user behaviors. But they can also
go further and measure the performance of the system and reject changes
if certain goals are not met.
\end{block}

\begin{block}{Performance testing}
\protect\phantomsection\label{performance-testing}
Performance tests evaluate how a system performs under a particular
workload. These tests help to measure the reliability, speed,
scalability, and responsiveness of an application. For instance, a
performance test can observe response times when executing a high number
of requests, or determine how a system behaves with a significant amount
of data. It can determine if an application meets performance
requirements, locate bottlenecks, measure stability during peak traffic,
and more. \#\# Smoke testing Smoke tests are basic tests that check the
basic functionality of an application. They are meant to be quick to
execute, and their goal is to give you the assurance that the major
features of your system are working as expected. Smoke tests can be
useful right after a new build is made to decide whether or not you can
run more expensive tests, or right after a deployment to make sure that
they application is running properly in the newly deployed environment.
\end{block}

\begin{block}{Fuzz testing}
\protect\phantomsection\label{fuzz-testing}
Fuzz testing, or fuzzing, is a type of automated testing that involves
providing invalid, unexpected, or random data as inputs to a computer
program. The program is then monitored for crashes, memory leaks, or
other unexpected behaviors. Fuzz testing is particularly useful for
identifying security vulnerabilities and robustness issues in software.
\end{block}
\end{frame}
